title: TOPROL-XL (metoprolol succinate) extended-release tablets, for oral use: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved prescribing information, initial US approval 1992; DailyMed structured product labelling version 7, published 6 March 2026
funder: not stated; FDA-approved labelling carries no funding statement. The labeller submits the text and the Food and Drug Administration approves it; TOPROL-XL is a trademark of the AstraZeneca group of companies and the tablets are manufactured by AstraZeneca AB.
result: Indications: hypertension, long-term treatment of angina pectoris, and heart failure, to reduce the risk of cardiovascular mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation. Starting doses are 25 to 100 mg daily for hypertension, 100 mg daily for angina and 12.5 or 25 mg daily for heart failure, doubled every two weeks to the highest tolerated dose or 200 mg. Mechanism: a beta1-selective (cardioselective) adrenergic receptor blocking agent without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; the preferential effect is not absolute and at higher plasma concentrations metoprolol also inhibits beta2 adrenoceptors, chiefly in bronchial and vascular musculature; relative beta1-selectivity diminishes and beta2 blockade increases above a plasma concentration of 300 nmol/l. Animal and human experiments indicate that metoprolol slows the sinus rate and decreases atrioventricular nodal conduction; beta1-blocking effects of 30% to 80% of maximum, an 8% to 23% reduction in exercise heart rate, correspond to plasma concentrations of 30 to 540 nmol/l. The mechanism of the antihypertensive effect has not been elucidated, and the precise mechanism of benefit in heart failure has not been elucidated. Pharmacokinetics: average bioavailability of the extended-release tablet 77% relative to conventional metoprolol across 50 to 400 mg once daily; peak plasma levels after conventional tablets approximate 50% of those after intravenous administration, indicating about 50% first-pass metabolism; about 12% is bound to serum albumin; metoprolol is a racemic mixture primarily metabolised by CYP2D6 with stereoselective metabolism dependent on oxidation phenotype; plasma half-life ranges from about 3 to 7 hours and less than 5% of an oral dose is recovered unchanged in the urine, the rest as metabolites with no beta-blocking activity. Pharmacogenomics: CYP2D6 is absent in about 8% of Caucasians (poor metabolisers) and about 2% of most other populations, and poor metabolisers have several-fold higher metoprolol blood levels, decreasing cardioselectivity; quinidine 100 mg with immediate-release metoprolol 200 mg tripled the concentration of S-metoprolol and doubled the elimination half-life in extensive metabolisers, and propafenone 150 mg three times daily raised steady-state metoprolol 2- to 5-fold. Warnings: following abrupt cessation of certain beta-blocking agents, exacerbations of angina pectoris and, in some cases, myocardial infarction have occurred, so the dosage is reduced gradually over 1 to 2 weeks with monitoring, treatment is promptly reinstated if angina markedly worsens, and abrupt discontinuation is avoided even in patients treated only for hypertension; bradycardia including sinus pause, heart block and cardiac arrest have occurred; beta-blockers may prevent early warning signs of hypoglycaemia such as tachycardia and increase the risk for severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially in diabetes, children and patients who are fasting; beta-adrenergic blockade may mask signs of hyperthyroidism and abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm; patients with bronchospastic disease should in general not receive beta-blockers. In the MERIT-HF study, 10.3% of patients on this product and 12.2% on placebo discontinued for adverse reactions, with dizziness or vertigo in 1.8% against 1.0% and bradycardia in 1.5% against 0.4%; in a randomised trial of 8351 patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery, 100 mg started 2 to 4 hours before surgery and continued at 200 mg daily for 30 days raised bradycardia (6.6% against 2.4%), hypotension (15% against 9.7%), stroke (1.0% against 0.5%) and death (3.1% against 2.3%).
